item.text: I’ll address counsel’s two claims in the reply and give Ray a direct signing recommendation. The supplied installer facts and the draft’s full-price §4.12 cap make this a decision worth spelling out plainly.

# Draft reply to J. Whitaker

Subject: Brightline APA — Schedule 3.3, WARN and §7.4(c)

J.,

Schedule 3.3 cannot read “None.” Hensley Homes’ MSA §18 requires its prior written consent to assignment, expressly including a sale of assets; it permits consent to be withheld in Hensley’s sole discretion and states an unauthorized assignment is void. Hensley accounts for 38% of Brightline’s reported $4.6 million 2025 revenue, or $1.748 million (0.38 × $4.6 million). The shop lease §22 also requires landlord consent, although it may not be unreasonably withheld. We propose both written consents as closing conditions. Cascade Builders’ framework agreement permits assignment to a successor to substantially all assets on notice, so it calls for notice and confirmation that Buyer qualifies, rather than consent. The City of Austin spray-booth permit is nontransferable and requires Buyer’s new application, with a stated 30–60 day processing period; it is a separate operating/closing timing issue, not a consent. We will populate Schedule 3.3 accordingly. The 22 smaller residential contracts are described as silent on assignment; we are reviewing their complete terms. The assignment position follows [the library’s assignment authority](../library/anti_assignment_change_of_control.md).

On WARN, the supplied census shows 14 W-2 employees. Even treating all nine 1099 installers as employees produces 23 people (14 + 9), below the federal 100-employee employer threshold; it is also below the 50-person site event threshold. On these supplied facts, Brightline is not a covered employer and a Brightline WARN notice is not required. The library states Texas has no mini-WARN statute. This answers Brightline’s headcount only; we have no census for Buyer or affiliated employers and cannot confirm their separate notice obligations. The underlying 1099 classification issue remains and must be disclosed and allocated in the APA. [WARN thresholds](../library/warn_act.md); [worker classification](../library/worker_classification_tx_irs.md).

We do not accept current §7.4(c). Its “acquired (or capable of being acquired) ... at any time” wording preserves an indemnity claim even where Buyer knew the particular inaccuracy before closing. We propose that actual, conscious pre-closing knowledge of the specific breach by Buyer’s transaction decision-makers bar the corresponding general-representation claim, with Seller bearing the burden of proof; constructive or merely available information would not count. A fact expressly excepted on a disclosure schedule would be outside the representation regardless of knowledge. The nine installers will be expressly excepted from §4.12, with any pre-closing exposure addressed by a separately negotiated, capped special indemnity that §7.4(c) would not cut off. The current full-purchase-price §4.12 cap is not acceptable. These are seller positions reflected in our proposed redline, rather than claims that either knowledge approach is universally “market standard.” [Sandbagging](../library/sandbagging.md); [baskets and caps](../library/baskets_caps.md).

We can work toward signing in two weeks, subject to agreement on the schedules, installer risk allocation, and the consent/permit timetable. We cannot represent that Hensley or the landlord will consent by that date, or that the new permit will issue then.

Regards,

Seller counsel
# Ray — three things that could cost you after closing

1. **The nine 1099 installers.** The facts look like employees: Brightline sets their daily work, supplies trucks and tools, pays hourly, and has been their exclusive source of work for years. “Everyone does it” does not decide their status. The draft makes you promise classification was proper and lets Buyer claim up to the full purchase price. The nine received $612,000 in 2025, or $68,000 each on average ($612,000 ÷ 9); that is a payment figure, **not** an estimate of tax or wage liability. We need to disclose them in the schedule, remove the clean promise for these nine, and cap any specific pre-closing claim. Buyer must handle classification after closing. [Classification](../library/worker_classification_tx_irs.md); [caps](../library/baskets_caps.md).

2. **The $400,000 earn-out may pay very little.** Buyer’s draft lets Buyer calculate EBITDA under its own policies. Your 2025 seller-prepared EBITDA was $740,000, which would yield only $16,000 under the formula if repeated and accepted as the earn-out measure: 40% × ($740,000 − $700,000). The $400,000 maximum needs $1,700,000 EBITDA ($700,000 + $400,000 ÷ 40%). We need a written calculation schedule, limits on Buyer charges, access to records, and a neutral accountant for disputes. The $180,000 salary and $42,000 legal add-backs also need agreed treatment. [Earn-out drafting](../library/earnout_definitions.md).

3. **The escrow is not the same as a liability limit.** Buyer would hold $310,000 for 18 months. That is 10% of an implied $3.1 million price ($310,000 ÷ 10%); the full price is inferred from the draft, not otherwise verified. As written, the installer representation carries a full-price cap, and Buyer can claim even if it knew of the problem. We propose making the escrow the only source for ordinary and specifically capped installer claims, except fundamental-representation claims, and agreeing when installer reserves are released. The Hensley customer contract and shop lease also need written consents; Hensley can refuse in its sole discretion, so do not let the sale close as though its revenue will automatically transfer. Hensley is $1.748 million of reported revenue (38% × $4.6 million). [Caps](../library/baskets_caps.md); [sandbagging](../library/sandbagging.md); [assignment](../library/anti_assignment_change_of_control.md).

**Before signing:** settle the contractor schedule and indemnity, the earn-out calculation, Hensley and landlord consent conditions, and the buyer’s plan for a new spray-booth permit. The permit is nontransferable and its stated reapplication time is 30–60 days, beyond the two-week signing target.
# Sandbagging clauses — pro- and anti-sandbagging

*Citation:* Delaware/Texas practice; *Akorn v. Fresenius* (Del. Ch. 2018) (dicta); ABA Private Target Deal Points Study  
*Status in this library:* in force

**Pro-sandbagging** clause: buyer may recover for breach of a representation even if it knew of the inaccuracy before signing/closing. **Anti-sandbagging**: buyer may not recover for breaches it knew of. Sellers who disclose a known issue (e.g., contractor classification) in diligence and then give a clean representation subject to a pro-sandbagging clause have effectively agreed to indemnify for the disclosed issue. The seller's protection is either (i) an anti-sandbagging clause, (ii) a disclosure schedule exception to the representation, or (iii) a special indemnity with a negotiated cap — not a clean rep.
# Worker classification — IRS common-law test; Texas Workforce Commission; successor exposure

*Citation:* IRS Rev. Rul. 87-41 (20 factors); Treas. Reg. §31.3121(d)-1; IRC §3509; Tex. Lab. Code §201.041; 40 TAC §815.134  
*Status in this library:* in force

Individuals who work exclusively for one business, on its schedule, with its tools and vehicles, paid hourly, for years, are employees under the common-law control test regardless of the label. Exposure: employer FICA/FUTA (§3509 reduced rates if non-willful), state unemployment tax, overtime under the FLSA (hourly, >40 hrs), benefits eligibility, workers' comp. In an **asset sale**, the buyer generally does not inherit the seller's pre-closing payroll-tax liabilities, but may inherit **FLSA liability as a successor** where there is substantial continuity, and will have to reclassify going forward — which is why buyers price it and demand indemnity.
# Indemnity baskets and caps — deductible vs tipping; survival

*Citation:* ABA Deal Points Study (private targets); market summary  
*Status in this library:* in force

A **deductible** basket: seller pays only losses above the threshold. A **tipping** basket: once the threshold is crossed, seller pays from the first dollar. Market: cap ~10% of price for general reps; fundamental reps and taxes to purchase price; **a specific operational rep (like worker classification) carved out to a full-price cap is off-market and should be resisted or replaced with a sized special indemnity**. Survival 12–24 months general.

item.text:
Ray should **not sign the current draft**. The nine installers’ working arrangements strongly indicate employee status, so a clean §4.12 compliance promise could expose him to a claim capped at the full purchase price. Counsel’s claim that §7.4(c) appears in every deal does not resolve that risk; the supplied reference library recognizes both knowledge approaches.

A two-week signing remains possible if the agreement first includes an express installer disclosure and capped indemnity, agreed earn-out accounting, and closing conditions for the Hensley and landlord consents and the new spray-booth permit. I updated the [reply to buyer’s counsel](/work/workspace/deliverable/reply_to_buyer_counsel.md) and [note to Ray](/work/workspace/deliverable/note_to_ray.md) with that position.
